title: Count Legal Piece Arrangements (Backtracking)
real_world_story: A board game engine must set up puzzles and validate starting positions. Some squares of the board are unusable, and no two rooks may share a row or a column, so the engine has to count every arrangement that keeps the position legal.

real_world_connection.input_represents: Board grid where '.' is an allowed square and 'X' is a forbidden square
real_world_connection.query_represents: The number of rooks K that must be placed
real_world_connection.algorithm_represents: Trying a square for each rook, rejecting rows and columns that are already occupied, and undoing the choice to try the next square

problem_statement: Given an N x N board of '.' (allowed) and 'X' (forbidden) and an integer K, count the distinct ways of placing exactly K non-attacking rooks. No two rooks may share a row or a column, no rook may stand on a forbidden square, and two arrangements are different when the set of occupied squares is different.
task: Return the number of legal arrangements of exactly K rooks. When K is 0 the empty arrangement counts as one arrangement.
input_format: The first line contains two integers N and K. The next N lines each contain N characters ('.' or 'X').
output_format: Print the number of legal arrangements.
constraints: Board cells are allowed (.) or forbidden (X)

examples.explanation: There are 3 choices of two rows and 3 choices of two columns. For each of those 9 pairs the two rooks can be placed in 2 ways, so 3 * 3 * 2 = 18 arrangements exist.

expected_algorithm.name: Backtracking
expected_algorithm.reason: Rooks are placed row by row, a square is accepted only when its column is still free and allowed, and each placement is undone so the next option can be tried.

complexity.time: O(N!) with pruning, because each row either stays empty or takes one of the free columns
complexity.space: O(N) for the used-column flags and the recursion

hint: Handle one row at a time and either leave it empty or put a rook in one allowed column.
Keep a flag per column so two rooks never share a column.
Stop a branch as soon as the remaining rows cannot hold the rooks that are still missing.
real_world_takeaway: Backtracking with a cheap constraint check counts every legal arrangement without ever enumerating arrangements that break the rules.
